1). Decrease in interlining - Certain parties have alleged that expansion of the commercial zone and terminal area formula will result in a decrease in the number of interline operations for long-haul carriers which are currently required. The following is an example which has been cited. Until recently, Rockville, Md., was not included in the Washington, D.C., terminal area. If an interstate carrier with authority between Chicago, Ill., and Washington, D.C., had a shipment from Chicago bound for Rockville, it would be required to enter the Washington terminal area and transfer its shipment to another carrier (usually a local or short-haul carrier) with authority to serve Rockville from Washington. Once Rockville was included in the Washington terminal zone, this shipment could be made directly to Rockville with the same authority, thus eliminating the need for an interline in Washington, and perhaps an empty backnaul on the part of the local carrier from Rockville back to Washington.
Similar results can be expected for any given city should the commercial zone and terminal area formula be expanded. Such a scenario would involvé a beneficial environmental impact in terms of air pollution, fuel consumption, and traffic congestion. Expansion of terminal areas would have the effect of decreasing the mileage as well as the number of hauls to make deliveries in certain instances. This would, in turn, reduce the fuel consumption of regulated carriers as well as the amount of air pollution emittants. Similarly, this action would remove from the urban and suburban highways and streets a number of trucks, thus reducing traffic congestion in these areas.
